title: TradFi doesn’t want DeFi. It wants blockchain.
gist: TradFi isn't converging with DeFi; it's selectively extracting blockchain's cost/settlement/programmability benefits while discarding open access, pseudonymity, and trustless execution, giving rise to a new institutional-only category the author calls 'programmable financial infrastructure.'

insights.claim: TradFi is not merging with DeFi; institutions are selectively using the parts of DeFi that fit their operating constraints and discarding the rest, reconfiguring the technology around institutional requirements rather than adopting its ethos.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Investors betting on a full DeFi/TradFi convergence narrative should instead model institutional blockchain adoption as a cost/infrastructure play, not a decentralization play.
insights.quote: Instead, they’re selectively using the parts of DeFi that fit within their operating constraints and discarding the parts that do not; they’re reconfiguring DeFi around institutional requirements.
insights.locator: There’s a version of the future that’s become almost canonical in crypto

insights.claim: Institutions adopt a blockchain primitive only when it simultaneously improves cost, risk, or distribution and remains compatible with control and accountability; primitives that fail the control test get rejected however elegant they are.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Builders can use this two-part test as a pre-screen for whether a given DeFi feature is institutionally sellable before spending resources adapting it.
insights.quote: TradFi adopts a primitive when it does two things at once: improves cost, risk, or distribution and stays compatible with control and accountability.
insights.locator: What TradFi is actually doing

insights.claim: The specific DeFi primitives institutions discard — open access, pseudonymity, and immutable execution — pass the cost/efficiency test but fail the control/accountability test, which is why the pattern of institutional adoption is predictable rather than arbitrary.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Product teams targeting institutions should design around retaining these three properties as optional/removable rather than core.
insights.locator: The primitives that institutions discard

insights.claim: JPM's permissioned blockchain for institutional deposits and the tokenized money-market funds run by BlackRock and Franklin Templeton are not toe-dips into DeFi; they use blockchain's programmability, transparency, and atomic settlement while deliberately discarding DeFi's open access, pseudonymity, and trustless execution.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Treat these deployments as evidence of the 'better plumbing, not decentralization' thesis — a template for what institutional blockchain products should look like.
insights.quote: These are deployments that use blockchains’ technical properties (programmability, transparency, atomic settlement) and deliberately discard the properties that make native DeFi work (open access, pseudonymity, and trustless execution).
insights.locator: So let’s be precise about what’s happening with initiatives like JPM’s permissioned blockchain

themes.theme: A new institutional category: programmable financial infrastructure

insights.claim: A new category built on blockchain rails but optimized for institutional constraints is emerging, distinct from both traditional finance and today's DeFi — the author terms it 'programmable financial infrastructure.'
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: This is a distinct investable category from both TradFi fintech and crypto-native DeFi — worth tracking as its own sector with its own comps.
insights.quote: we’re beginning to see the emergence of a new category built on blockchain rails but optimized for institutional constraints: programmable financial infrastructure.
insights.locator: What this means is that institutions aren’t somehow merging with DeFi

insights.claim: Legislation such as the CLARITY Act could eventually make it easier for institutions to engage directly with permissionless systems, but institutions' risk posture will not reset overnight even after favorable regulatory change.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Don't expect a regulatory unlock (e.g. CLARITY Act passage) to trigger an immediate rush of institutional capital into permissionless DeFi — the risk-culture lag will persist.
insights.quote: regardless of what becomes legally possible, TradFi’s risk posture won’t reset overnight.
insights.locator: That dynamic may evolve as regulatory frameworks mature

insights.claim: The industry has two parallel, non-competing opportunities: helping institutions adopt the blockchain infrastructure they're ready for today, and continuing to build the open, crypto-native financial system institutions aren't yet prepared to use.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Allocators can use this as a two-bucket framework for categorizing crypto infrastructure bets: institutional-adoption plays vs. open-network innovation plays.
insights.locator: which is why this presents the industry with two opportunities, not one

insights.claim: Institutions reconfigure DeFi along two axes: compliance (KYC, AML, sanctions screening, investor accreditation, the ability to freeze/reverse transactions and identify counterparties) and enterprise value delivery (cost compression, reconciliation reduction, new distribution channels, deeper customer embedding).
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Use these two axes as a due-diligence checklist when evaluating whether an institutional-facing crypto product will clear procurement.
insights.locator: The reconfiguration happens along two axes

insights.claim: Enterprises historically reshape new technologies to fit existing risk and procurement processes rather than adopting them in original form — seen with the internet (firewalls, private intranets), cloud computing (private cloud, VPCs, FedRAMP), and AI (internal deployments, data residency requirements, model governance) — and blockchain is following the same pattern.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Expect a 'permissioned/private' variant of blockchain infrastructure to become the dominant institutional form factor, analogous to VPC/private-cloud in the cloud-computing analogy.
insights.quote: It happened with the internet (enterprise firewalls, private intranets). It happened with cloud computing (private cloud, VPCs, FedRAMP). It’s happening with AI (internal deployments, data residency requirements, model governance). Blockchain is no different.
insights.locator: Any technology that enters a heavily regulated, risk-managed, liability-averse institutional environment

themes.theme: Stablecoins, Circle, and SWIFT as case studies

insights.claim: Stablecoins are the clearest example of selective adoption: banks, payment providers, and fintechs value them as settlement infrastructure for faster cross-border dollar movement, not because they embrace permissionless-finance philosophy.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Stablecoin infrastructure plays targeting banks/fintechs should be positioned as settlement-speed tools, not as gateways to DeFi philosophy — the buyer doesn't care about the latter.
insights.quote: They’re adopting programmable dollars because they’re useful, not because they’re trying to recreate the financial system around DeFi’s principles.
insights.locator: Stablecoins may be the clearest example

insights.claim: Circle's Arc product illustrates how blockchain infrastructure is being repackaged for institutional buyers, emphasizing compliance, operational controls, and trusted counterparties over permissionless access and composability, with the value proposition centered on faster settlement, global reach, and capital efficiency.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Circle's Arc is a concrete reference product for what a winning institutional-grade blockchain offering looks like — useful comp for evaluating competing infra startups.
insights.quote: Arc reflects how blockchain infrastructure is increasingly being packaged for institutional buyers: emphasizing compliance, operational controls, trusted counterparties, and integration into existing workflows rather than permissionless access and composability.
insights.locator: Circle’s evolution is an apt illustration

insights.claim: SWIFT's tokenized-asset-interoperability efforts are aimed at helping existing financial institutions coordinate better with one another via the SWIFT network, not at displacing incumbents — an example of blockchain adoption strengthening rather than replacing established financial networks.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Incumbent financial-market infrastructure (SWIFT-like networks) is a plausible long-term winner of blockchain adoption, not just a disruption target — relevant for positioning against 'SWIFT killer' crypto narratives.
insights.quote: Blockchain adoption that strengthens established financial networks rather than displacing them.
insights.locator: Even organizations like SWIFT increasingly frame blockchain through this lens

themes.theme: Builder strategy: pick one lane, converge at the rails

insights.claim: Institutional and open-network crypto businesses require fundamentally different go-to-market skills — procurement, compliance, controls, channel partners, and long sales cycles versus developers, liquidity, composability, and network effects — so while the industry can pursue both opportunities in parallel, a single company should not try to pursue both at once.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: When evaluating crypto startups, penalize teams that claim to serve both institutional and crypto-native customers simultaneously with one product/GTM motion — the article argues this is a mistake.
insights.quote: At the industry level, it would be a mistake for everyone to abandon one opportunity for the other. At the company level, it would be a mistake to try to pursue both at once.
insights.locator: Two opportunities for builders

insights.claim: Convergence between TradFi and DeFi, if it happens, will occur at the level of shared rails — public blockchains as neutral settlement — rather than through one system absorbing or replacing the other.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Value accrual in convergence scenarios should be modeled at the base settlement/rails layer rather than assuming winner-take-all between DeFi apps and TradFi apps.
insights.quote: Convergence, when it comes, happens at the rails — not by one system surrendering to the other.
insights.locator: Partnering with institutions and building an adjacent financial system aren’t in tension

insights.claim: Public blockchains may become increasingly important as neutral settlement rails even as the applications built on top of them become progressively more permissioned, implying a bifurcation between an open infrastructure layer and an increasingly closed application layer.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Investors should distinguish base-layer blockchain exposure (likely to stay open/neutral) from application-layer exposure (likely to trend permissioned/institutional) when constructing a crypto infrastructure thesis.
insights.quote: Public blockchains may become increasingly important settlement rails, even as the applications built on top of them become progressively more permissioned.
insights.locator: This doesn’t mean one opportunity is better than the other

themes.theme: Build-from-scratch vs. adapt-existing: Canton and Morpho

insights.claim: Canton exemplifies the build-from-scratch approach to institutional blockchain infrastructure: rather than adapting existing DeFi protocols, it is designed specifically around institutional requirements for privacy, compliance, and controlled interoperability.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Canton is a reference case for the 'purpose-built institutional network' strategy, useful as a comp when evaluating similarly positioned infrastructure projects.
insights.locator: Consider networks like Canton

insights.claim: Morpho exemplifies the adapt-existing approach: it kept its DeFi lending primitives but made them easier for institutions and asset issuers to consume; Apollo's ACRED fund uses Morpho as part of its onchain lending strategy, pairing a DeFi-native primitive with institutional-grade distribution, compliance, and fund structure.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Morpho/Apollo's ACRED is a concrete precedent for how a DeFi-native protocol can be repackaged as institutional infrastructure without abandoning its core primitives — useful as a template for other DeFi protocols seeking institutional distribution.
insights.quote: Apollo’s ACRED fund, for example, uses Morpho as part of its onchain lending strategy, pairing a DeFi- native lending primitive with institutional-grade distribution, compliance, and fund structures.
insights.locator: Not every successful institutional strategy requires rebuilding from scratch

insights.claim: Adapting crypto-native infrastructure for institutions, as Morpho did, is not the default playbook; in many cases designing a product for institutional requirements from the outset will be more effective than retrofitting an open-network product.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Founders shouldn't default to 'adapt our DeFi protocol for institutions' as the go-to strategy — greenfield institutional-native builds may be the better bet in many cases.
insights.quote: But builders shouldn’t mistake this for the default playbook. Institutions are a distinct customer segment with distinct requirements.
insights.locator: Some teams, like Morpho, have successfully adapted crypto-native infrastructure

insights.claim: Institutions are not the crypto industry's primary source of innovation; the permissioned layer is downstream of the open layer, and the innovations institutions are adopting today did not originate inside banks or asset managers but emerged from open networks experimenting freely with new market structures.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Track open-network / DeFi-native experimentation as a leading indicator of what institutional infrastructure will look like 2-3 years out, rather than watching bank pilots for signal.
insights.quote: Institutions are not the industry’s primary source of innovation: The permissioned layer is often downstream from the open one.
insights.locator: The innovations institutions are adopting today did not originate inside banks

insights.claim: The industry risks mistaking a large buyer category for the entire opportunity if it becomes too focused on selling to banks and asset managers; institutional adoption is a large opportunity but not simply an extension of DeFi, and success in one market doesn't guarantee success in the other.
insights.speaker: Christian Crowley
insights.so_what: Portfolio construction should avoid over-rotating entirely into institutional-facing crypto infrastructure at the expense of open-network bets, since the two markets have separate success criteria.
insights.quote: If our industry becomes too focused on selling to banks and asset managers, we risk mistaking a large buyer category for the entire opportunity.
insights.locator: This brings us to the more important strategic point
